{{Shinto}}{{Expand Japanese|date=May 2022}}The {{Nihongo|'''Association of Shinto Shrines'''|神社本庁|Association of Shinto Shrines}} is a religious administrative organisation that oversees about 80,000 {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}}s in {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}}. These shrines take the [[Ise Grand Shrine]] as the foundation of their belief. It is the largest [[Shrine Shinto]] organization in existence.
== Description ==
The association has five major activities, in addition to numerous others:<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/en/about/|title = Jinja-Honcho -CIVILIZATION OF THE DIVINE FOREST-}}</ref>
*Publication and dissemination of information on [[Shrine Shinto]]
*The performance of rituals;
*Education of adherents to Shinto;
*Reverence of Ise Grand Shrine and the distribution of its [[Ofuda|amulets]] called ''[[:en:Jingū Taima|Jingū Taima]]'' ([[:ja:神宮大麻|神宮大麻]]); and
*Preparation and training of individuals for the [[kannushi|Shinto priesthood]].
It currently has an administrative structure including a main office and branches. Its headquarters in {{ill|Yoyogi|en|Yoyogi|qid=Q1190291|lt=Yoyogi}}, {{ill|Shibuya|en|Shibuya|qid=Q193638|lt=Shibuya}}, {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|qid=Q1490|lt=Tokyo}}, adjacent to [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]]. Its leadership includes the {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Sosai|Sosai]]''|総裁}}, the head priestess of the Ise Shrine, presently {{ill|Sayako Kuroda|en|Sayako Kuroda|qid=Q229333|lt=Sayako Kuroda}}.<ref>[https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2017/06/21/national/politics-diplomacy/emperors-daughter-becomes-supreme-priestess-ise-shrine/#.WbR-zJQhXqA Japan Times]</ref> The {{Nihongo|''tōri''|統理}} is {{ill|Kuniaki Kuni|ja|久邇邦昭|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kuniaki Kuni|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11369705}}, and the post of {{Nihongo|''sōchō''|総長}} or Secretary-General is currently held by [[Masami Yatabe]], the chief priest of the [[Mishima Taisha|Mishima Shrine]].  The association maintains regional offices in every {{ill|Prefectures of Japan|en|Prefectures of Japan|qid=Q50337|lt=prefecture}}. They handle financial and personnel matters for member shrines.
== Overview ==
The Association of Shinto Shrines is the largest Shinto religious group in Japan, and more than 79,000 of the approximately 80,000 Japanese shrines, including major ones, are members.<ref name="nenkan">[https://www.bunka.go.jp/tokei_hakusho_shuppan/hakusho_nenjihokokusho/shukyo_nenkan/pdf/h19nenkan.pdf 『宗教年鑑』平成19th year ] 2-4ページ</ref> Each prefecture has a shrine office <ref>[http://www.jinjahoncho.or.jp/introduction/jinjacho/ 神社本庁 神社庁一覧]</ref>{{r|nenkan}}. It is the successor to the {{ill|Institute of Divinities|en|Institute of Divinities|qid=Q11590709|lt=Institute of Divinities}}, which was an external agency of the {{ill|Home Ministry|en|Home Ministry|qid=Q1142265|lt=Home Ministry}},<ref>{{Cite web |title=神社庁とは |url=https://www.okayama-jinjacho.or.jp/about/jinjacho/ |website=岡山県神社庁 |accessdate=2020-05-04}}</ref> and is a comprehensive [[religious corporation]] based on the Religious Corporation Law.
In Article 3 of the "Regulations of the Religious Corporation 'Jinja Honcho' Agency," the regulations of the Agency as a religious corporation, the purpose of the Agency is to manage and guide shrines under its jurisdiction, promote Shinto, perform shrine rituals, educate and foster believers ([[Ujigami|Ujiko]]), support [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]], the head shrine, train priests, and conduct public relations through the publication and distribution of pamphlets, among other activities. The shrine is also involved in public relations activities through the publication and distribution of pamphlets.
== Doctrine ==
=== Association of Shinto Shrine Charter ===
The Association of Shinto Shrines is a comprehensive religious corporation of about 80,000 companies nationwide. Each shrine has its own history, and there are various religious beliefs such as Yawata belief and Inari belief, and it was very difficult to establish one doctrine. Therefore, on May 21, 1980 (Showa 55), the "Association of Shinto Shrine Charter" was established by a decision of the Councilors. The background and position of this is stated in the preamble, "The important concern to date has been to establish and maintain basic norms as a tie for spiritual integration." At the time of enforcement of this Charter, the agency rules and previous rules, etc. shall be deemed to have been established based on this Charter."
Article 1 states, "The Association of Shinto Shrines respects tradition, promotes rituals and promotes morality, prays for the prosperity of the great lord, and contributes to the peace of the four seas."
=== Platform for Respectful Life ===
Prior to the "Association of Shinto Shrine Charter", the "Platform of Respectful Life" was enacted in 1956 to show the practical spirit of the Association of Shinto Shrines.
{{Quote|text=Shinto is an eternal road of heaven and earth, and is the basis for cultivating a noble spirit and opening the Taihei.
It is the reason for achieving the mission to be afraid of the gods, to follow the ancestral lessons, to
finally demonstrate the essence of the road,
and to promote the welfare of humankind.
It is hoped that this code will be put up here to clarify the direction and to put it into practice and proclaim the road.
To thank God for the grace and grace of our ancestors, to attend rituals with a clear and clean
spirit, to serve for the sake of the world, and to create and solidify the world as the will of God.
We pray for the coexistence and co-prosperity of the country and the world.}}
There is no codified doctrine in the Association of Shinto Shrines, but according to the "Commentary on the Charter of the Association of Shinto Shrines", the Association of Shinto Shrines is the spirit of its establishment and activities with the "Association of Shinto Shrines" and the "Platform of Respectful Life".<ref>神社本庁教学研究室編『神社本庁憲章の解説』神社本庁、1985</ref>
== History ==
The Association was established following the {{ill|Surrender of Japan|en|Surrender of Japan|qid=Q6540361|lt=Surrender of Japan}} at the end of {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}. On 15 December 1945, the [[Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers]] (SCAP) issued the ''[[Shinto Directive]]'', ordering the [[:en:Disestablishment|Disestablishment]] of Shinto as a {{ill|State religion|en|State religion|qid=Q188213|lt=State religion}}. On February 2, 1946, to comply with the SCAP order, three organizations – the {{Nihongo|Kōten Kōkyūjo|皇典講究所}}, {{Nihongo|Dainippon Jingikai|大日本神祇会}}, and {{Nihongo|Jingū Hōsaikai|神宮奉斎会}} – established the nongovernmental Association, assuming the functions of the {{ill|Institute of Divinities|en|Institute of Divinities|qid=Q11590709|lt=Institute of Divinities}}, a branch of the [[:en:Home Ministry (Japan)|Home Ministry]].
In accordance with the [[Shinto Directive]], {{ill|1946|en|1946|qid=Q18610|lt=1946}} ([[:en:Shōwa (1926-1989)|Showa]]21) {{ill|January 23|en|January 23|qid=Q2276|lt=January 23}}, {{ill|National Association of Shinto Priests|en|National Association of Shinto Priests|qid=Q11389505|lt=National Association of Shinto Priests}}, the [[:en:Office of Japanese Classics Research|Office of Japanese Classics Research]], and the [[Jingūkyō]], took the lead to establish the Jinja Honcho.{{Sfn|中山|2009|p=231}}{{Sfn|文化庁編さん|2011|pp=54-61}}
=== Political links ===
The Association has many contacts within the {{ill|Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|en|Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|qid=Q232595|lt=Liberal Democratic Party}} and is a successful [[lobbyist]]; its influence can be seen in recent conservative legislation, like the legal recognition of the National Flag ({{ill|Flag of Japan|en|Flag of Japan|qid=Q43175|lt=Hinomaru}}) and National Anthem ([[Kimigayo]]), their use for official school events, or the revision of {{ill|Fundamental Law of Education|en|Fundamental Law of Education|qid=Q1037346|lt=Fundamental Education Law}}, and it is behind some actions by {{ill|Conservatism|en|Conservatism|qid=Q7169|lt=conservative}} {{ill|Politician|en|Politician|qid=Q82955|lt=Politician}}s, like visits to {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|en|Yasukuni Shrine|qid=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}} by [[:en:Junichirō Koizumi|Junichirō Koizumi]], then {{ill|Prime Minister of Japan|en|Prime Minister of Japan|qid=Q274948|lt=Prime Minister of Japan}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Secularization, Deprivatization, and the Reappearance of 'Public Religion' in Japanese Society|journal=Journal of Religion in Japan|volume=1|pages=61–82|doi=10.1163/221183412X628442|year=2012|last1=Mullins|first1=Mark R}}</ref>
